head:
Tests · Reading your results

Reading a norm table: age, sex, percentile

You take a test, you get a number, then a label: "average", "good", "62nd percentile". This article takes the label apart. Where does it come from, who does it compare you with, what can it tell you about your health, and how do you know whether you have really improved between two tests? We start from an isolated number and end with what to do with it.

The problem

A score on its own means nothing. A VO2max of 45 mL/kg/min, 2,000 metres in the Cooper test, 38 kg on the grip test: these numbers have no value until you know what to compare them with. That is the job of a norm table: a table that turns your raw number into a position (a percentile) or a label ("poor", "average", "excellent").

The problem is that the label looks objective. Yet it depends on three choices you did not make: the group you are compared with (age, sex), how that group was measured (which test, which population), and how the results are divided up (into ranks, or according to health risk). Two serious norm tables can give the same person two different labels.

A second difficulty comes after the test. You redo it two months later and the number has moved by a few points: progress, or measurement noise? And if your percentile goes from 40 to 55, has something changed in your body, or only in the table?

The question

What does a result ranked by age, sex and percentile mean: who does it really compare you with, what can be concluded about your health, and how do you know you have genuinely improved?

We answer in six steps, from the most general to the most precise: what a percentile is, the effect of age and sex, the biases of the norm table itself, the difference between a rank and a risk, measurement error, then comparing yourself with yourself.

What is at stake

The first issue is the decision you make based on the label. Placed in "average", you may ease off when your margin is narrow. Placed in "poor" because you were compared with a group twenty years younger, you may get discouraged, or push harder than you should.

The second is health. Studies on fitness rank people by level and link those levels to the risk of death. If your label overlaps with one of these levels, it has real-world relevance. If it only measures a rank in some arbitrary population, it does not. Knowing which of the two you are looking at changes what you do with it. For strength, British researchers present their grip strength reference curves as a way of helping clinicians spot sarcopenia and frailty: a poorly chosen norm risks missing cases or creating them (reasoning, not a study result).14

The third is follow-up over time. A test is only worth something if it tells you whether what you are doing works. Yet this is the most fragile part: measurement error can hide a small change, and a change of age bracket moves your percentile without your body having changed. We will see this with numbers.

The fourth is mental. A percentile reads like a ranking, and therefore like a judgement. Constantly comparing yourself with the "top 10%" without knowing which group is meant wears down motivation; understanding what the number measures lets you use it as a tool. The question cannot be left unanswered: the norm table is the interface between the test and your life.

Step 1 of 6 · A single group

An isolated number says nothing: you need a distribution

Let's take a concrete, real example. The FRIEND registry, in the United States, brought together 7,783 adults aged 20 to 79, free of cardiovascular disease, tested to exhaustion on a treadmill in eight laboratories between January 2014 and February 2015.1 For each ten-year age bracket and each sex, it publishes VO2max, that is, the maximum oxygen your body can use in one minute, relative to your weight, at several percentiles.

For men aged 20 to 29, the values are: 32.1 at the 10th percentile, 40.1 at the 25th, 48.0 at the 50th, 55.2 at the 75th and 61.8 at the 90th (in mL/kg/min).2 A percentile reads like this: the 25th percentile is the value below which 25% of the group lies. A 25-year-old man at 45 is therefore above about 40 people out of 100 of his age and sex, and below the other 60. The same 45 is neither good nor bad in itself: it is slightly below the median.

A percentile is a position on the bell curve, not a grade

Men aged 20 to 29, treadmill. The percentiles shown (10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th) are those of the FRIEND registry.2 The bell curve is a normal approximation drawn by us (mean 48.0, standard deviation 11.6, calculated from the 10th and 90th percentiles): it falls within about 1 mL/kg/min of the published percentiles. The percentage displayed is interpolated between the table values, so it is approximate.

What this means

A percentile does not grade your performance, it places it: how many people in this group do less than you. In the middle of the curve, a small difference in the number moves your position a lot; at the extremes, it takes a large one. Keep this idea in mind for step 5.

Mean, median, percentile

The mean is the sum divided by the number of people. The median is the middle value (the 50th percentile): half the group is below it. Any percentile generalises the idea: at the 75th, 75% of the group is below. In a symmetrical bell curve, mean and median coincide, hence the confusion. As soon as a few extreme values pull the distribution, they separate. The authors of a VO2max reference equation also note that existing norms do not follow a normal distribution and transfer poorly, especially for women: this is why registries publish percentiles.12

An extreme value moves the mean, not the median or the rank

Calculation example with invented numbers (40, 42, 44, 45, 47, 48 and a seventh, variable score), unrelated to any study. Percentile calculated here as the share of the seven people strictly below.

What this means

In this example, the person at 47 goes from "above the mean" to "below the mean" without their score or their rank having changed. A mean depends on everybody, extreme cases included; a rank does not. So check whether a norm table gives you percentiles (positions) or a mean (a centre).

A single group is enough to understand the mechanism. Let's see what happens when the group changes.

Step 2 of 6 · Groups that differ

Age and sex shift the reference

The same FRIEND registry gives percentiles for six age brackets, in men and in women. The following figure shows the median of each group and the zone running from the 10th to the 90th percentile.2 Note the dotted line: we come back to it in step 4.

The median falls with each age bracket, and the women's median is lower at every age

Men: median, zone from the 10th to the 90th percentileWomen: median, zone from the 10th to the 90th percentile

VO2max measured on a treadmill, FRIEND registry (7,783 adults without cardiovascular disease).1 Values reproduced from a secondary site, which cites the article by Kaminsky, Arena and Myers (Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 2015).2 The dotted line is derived: 7.9 METs (lower limit in the Kodama study)10 multiplied by 3.5 mL/kg/min per MET.11

Read the figure in three stages. Age first: in men the median goes from 48.0 at 20-29 years to 24.4 at 70-79 years, in women from 37.6 to 18.3, roughly half over five decades (calculation). A cycling study (4,494 tests) gives a similar order of magnitude: about a 10% decline per decade.3

Then sex. The median for women aged 20 to 29 (37.6) is almost the same as that of men aged 40 to 49 (37.8). The same 37.6 is therefore median for one, below the 25th percentile for a man of her age (40.1), and above the 90th for a woman aged 60 to 69 (27.0). The pages read describe these gaps without detailing their causes.2

Finally, the shape of the curve, which depends on the test. For grip strength, 12 British general-population studies (49,964 people) show strength that rises, stays at its peak (median of 51 kg in men between 29 and 39, 31 kg in women between 26 and 42), then declines from midlife.14 VO2max, by contrast, falls with every decade in the FRIEND table, with no visible plateau.

The same effect appears in field tests. In the 12-minute Cooper test table (reproduced by a sports testing site, attributed to Cooper 1968), 2,000 metres counts as "below average" for a man aged 20 to 29, "average" at 40 to 49 and "above average" at 50 and over. For a woman: "average" at 20-29, "above average" at 40-49.5 Three labels for the same 2,000 metres.

What this means

A raw number is never compared with "everyone": it is compared with people of the same sex and a similar age, and the label changes depending on the group. When a site gives you your percentile, check which group it puts you in.

Age and sex are well-documented reference choices. But we assumed that the table itself was reliable and unique. It is not.

Step 3 of 6 · The table itself

The norm table is itself a measurement, with its own biases

A reference table is the result of a study: a sample, a test, a period. Three published examples show the gap this creates.

Two tables for the same VO2max. The Garmin rankings, which reproduce Cooper Institute data with permission, give for men aged 20 to 29 a value of 41.7 at the 40th percentile and 45.4 at the 60th: the median lies between the two, around 43.6 (midpoint, estimate). FRIEND gives 48.0.4,2 For men aged 70 to 79: 29.4 and 32.3 (midpoint: about 30.9), against 24.4. For women aged 20 to 29, the tables agree (midpoint 37.8 against 37.6). The pages read do not describe the Cooper Institute sample: it is impossible to say why they diverge.

The test mode. On a cycle ergometer (4,494 tests), the medians at 20 to 29 are 41.9 in men and 31.0 in women, against 48.0 and 37.6 on a treadmill: 6.1 and 6.6 lower (differences between two studies).3,2 Field tests add another layer: a meta-analysis of 57 studies gives a correlation of 0.66 to 0.84 between the 20-metre shuttle run and VO2max, a "moderate to high" validity for an estimate, not a measurement.17

The equations. Wasserman's (1984) were based on a sample that specialists consider small and homogeneous, against more than 80,000 subjects for FRIEND.13 And a norm table gets revised: the secondary site that reproduces FRIEND mentions a 2022 update lowering the treadmill medians by 1.5 to 4.6 mL/kg/min. I could not open that article.2

The same number, two norm tables: choose a group and move the slider

Sources: FRIEND (treadmill, values reproduced by a secondary site)2 and Cooper Institute (table reproduced by Garmin; the categories are poor, fair, good, excellent, superior).4 The FRIEND percentage is interpolated between two table values, so it is approximate. For the Cooper Institute, the category begins at the threshold given in the table.

What this means

A percentile is not a property of you: it is a property of you and the table. A man aged 70 to 79 at 30 mL/kg/min is around the 73rd percentile in one table and "fair", between the 40th and 60th, in the other. So always note the name of the norm table, the test and the population.

Let's assume the right group and the right table. That leaves the question everyone asks: is it good? This is where the reasoning turns around.

Step 4 of 6 · Rank or risk

A percentile ranks, it does not judge: rank and risk are two questions

A norm table based on percentiles ranks people against each other; by construction, it says nothing about what is good for health. In the Cooper Institute table reproduced by Garmin, the "poor" category covers percentiles 0 to 40: 40% of the reference population is "poor", healthy or not.4

The health question is different: at what level does risk increase? At the Cleveland Clinic, 122,007 patients tested on a treadmill were classified by age and sex percentile (below the 25th, 25th to 49th, 50th to 74th, 75th to 97.6th, 97.7th and above), then followed for a median of 8.4 years.6 We look at what the class predicts.

In this cohort, each percentile class comes with a lower risk

Heights derived from published adjusted risk ratios: low versus below average 1.95,7 below average versus above average 1.41, elite versus high 0.77, low versus elite 5.04.6 Chaining: approximate. Thresholds in METs, 50 to 59 years: table 2 of the study. Patients from a single centre.

What this means

Here the percentile follows a risk gradient, and the biggest step is the first: from the low class to the next (ratio of 1.95). A cardiologist quoted by the specialist press (Lavie) sums it up: the biggest gain is getting out of the lowest level.7 Note also the thresholds, defined by sex: 8.1 METs is "low" for a man aged 50 to 59 (under 8.2) but "above average" for a woman of the same age (8.1 to 9.9).

A relative rank and an absolute risk threshold do not overlap, however. The Kodama meta-analysis (33 studies) set a "low" fitness at under 7.9 METs: these people had a 70% higher risk of death than those at 10.9 METs or more.10 One MET equals 3.5 mL/kg/min: 7.9 METs is about 27.7, the dotted line from step 2.11 The women's median falls below this line from 40-49 years (26.7), the men's from 70-79 years (24.4). A 75-year-old woman at the median of her group (18.3) is "average" for her age, far below a threshold defined without reference to age. This comparison should be treated with caution (METs often estimated, nominal conversion, different populations): it only shows that position and risk are two distinct pieces of information.

No universal numerical threshold exists: the authors of a 2024 review state this explicitly.11 In a cohort of 750,302 veterans, the least fit group (20th percentile) has a risk of death 4.09 times higher than the extremely fit group; the lowest risk, around 14 METs, is 0.24 in men and 0.23 in women.8 The same absolute level goes with a similar risk in both sexes: a cautious reading. An unverified secondary summary even states that risk thresholds fall with age, from 8 to 9 METs before 50 to 5 to 6 after 70.9

For grip strength, weakness is defined as 2.5 standard deviations below the peak mean of each sex, and therefore relative to young adults: at 80, 23% of men and 27% of women are below this threshold.14 In a normal distribution, this would correspond to about 0.6% of a group (calculation).

What this means

There are two readings. Rank: where am I among my peers? Threshold: am I above or below a level associated with a risk? Both are useful, for different questions. A "50th percentile" is neither good nor bad in itself. The studies read describe associations: they do not say that a shift in your percentile changes your health by a specific amount.

To track your progress with a norm table, you still need to be able to trust the measurement.

Step 5 of 6 · Measurement

Between two tests: measurement error and real progress

A percentile turns a difference in number into a difference in rank, unevenly. In men aged 40 to 49, FRIEND gives 31.9 at the 25th percentile and 37.8 at the 50th: 5.9 mL/kg/min for 25 ranks, or about 4 ranks per mL/kg/min. In the tails, it is about 2 ranks (8.0 to go from the 10th to the 25th in men aged 20 to 29, 6.6 from the 75th to the 90th; calculations).2 In the middle, where most people are, a small change moves the percentile a lot.

On top of this comes measurement noise. One study had 15 male amateur runners (mean age 34.5 years) do the 12-minute Cooper test twice, 48 hours apart: 3,026 then 3,047 metres on average, a mean difference of 20.46 metres (95% confidence interval of minus 20.22 to plus 61.15). The variation index in the table is 52.2 metres (1.7%), and the authors recommend not attributing a smaller change to training. The sample is small and trained, and the tests are only two days apart: it is a benchmark, not a constant.16

A 20-metre difference can change the label without changing anything about fitness

Imaginary example: a runner aged 40 to 49 who runs 2,090 m then 2,110 m (invented numbers). Categories of the 12-minute Cooper test for men aged 40 to 49, as reproduced by a sports testing site.5 The 52.2 m bar represents the threshold chosen by the authors of a study on 15 male amateur runners: a benchmark for this runner, not his own error.16

What this means

Here, 20 metres is enough to go from "average" to "above average", while the threshold chosen by the reliability study is 52.2 metres. The imaginary runner has changed nothing. A category band is 400 metres wide: 52.2 metres represent about 13% of it (calculation). The closer you are to a boundary, the more a change of label can be noise. Look at the number, not just the word.

What counts as progress? The 2024 review cites 1 MET (3.5 mL/kg/min) as the smallest clinically important difference.11 For a man aged 40 to 49, that is about 15 ranks in the middle of the distribution (calculation). In Kodama, each additional MET went with 13% lower mortality: an association between people, not a promise for you.10 A field test that estimates VO2max (correlation of 0.66 to 0.84) adds its own error.17 A change is only readable if it exceeds the error of your test, known only by redoing it under the same conditions.

Step 6 of 6 · Yourself, and the limits

Comparing yourself with yourself, and what remains uncertain

The most solid comparison is the one you make with yourself. A 1995 study followed 9,777 men tested twice, 4.9 years apart, then for 5.1 years (223 deaths). Death rates per 10,000 man-years, age-adjusted: 122.0 in those who stayed unfit, 67.7 in those who went from unfit to fit, 39.6 in those who stayed fit. Those who improved had a 44% lower risk than the men who stayed unfit (interval of 25 to 59%), and each additional minute on the treadmill went with 7.9% fewer deaths.15 The norm table plays no part: an individual is compared with himself.

This approach does not escape the age trap. A man at 37.8 mL/kg/min at 39 sits around the 32nd percentile of 30-39 year olds (interpolation between the 25th at 35.9 and the 50th at 42.4). At 40, with the same number, he is at the median of 40-49 year olds: about 18 ranks gained with no improvement at all (calculation).2 When the age bracket changes, compare the raw number, not the percentile.

The serious objections

The samples. FRIEND comes from laboratories, with people without cardiovascular disease, and the page read does not say that it is representative; the Cleveland cohort comes from a single centre.1,6 Causality. The risk studies are observational: a sick person does worse during exercise, and those who improve may change other habits.15,6 The sources. The FRIEND table, the age thresholds and the 12-minute Cooper table are secondary, as noted: for an individual decision, consult the original articles.

What this means

To track your progress, your own number, always measured the same way, is worth more than your percentile. The norm table is for placing you at a given moment. Follow-up over time is for knowing whether you are improving. The two are not read the same way and do not add up.

Answer to the question

The question was: what does a result ranked by age, sex and percentile mean, what can be concluded about your health, and how do you know you have improved? Here is the answer, with the level of certainty of each part.

What is solid. A percentile places your result in a specific group, no more, no less. Published reference groups differ enormously by age and sex: median VO2max is roughly halved between 20-29 years and 70-79 years, and that of women aged 20 to 29 is that of men aged 40 to 49. Two serious tables can diverge by about 6 mL/kg/min for the same group. A test-to-test difference smaller than the measurement noise proves nothing.

What is probable. Percentile classes follow a risk gradient in large cohorts, with the clearest gain on leaving the lowest class. A better level achieved over time goes with a lower risk, subject to the limits of observation. Your rank in your group and your level of risk are two different pieces of information, which partly overlap.

What is not established. There is no universal threshold for "good" or "low", and no study read shows that a specific shift in your percentile changes your health by a given amount. I could not assess the ACSM, EUROFIT and ALPHA-Fitness norm tables, as I had not opened them.

What to put in place

  1. Note the context of your test.Date, time, surface or device, warm-up, your weight, your age. Without this, the result cannot be compared with another, or with a norm table.
  2. Find your group: same sex, same age bracket, same type of test.Keep two things: your raw number and the name of the norm table used. A percentile without the name of the norm table is worthless for comparison.
  3. Read the percentile as a position, not a verdict.A 40th percentile means that 40 people out of 100 in your reference group do worse. For health, also check whether you are in the lowest class of the risk studies: that is where the expected gain is greatest.
  4. Find your error by redoing the test twice, two days apart.This follows the protocol of the Cooper test study. The difference you observe between the two attempts is a benchmark for your own noise: a change smaller than that difference is not progress.
  5. Then redo the test under the same conditions, at regular intervals, and follow the trend.Every 8 to 12 weeks is a practical choice, not a study result: none of the sources read sets a frequency. Do not conclude from a single difference; look at three points or more.
  6. When you change age bracket, compare the raw number.Your percentile can rise or fall without your fitness having moved. A very low score, chest pain or abnormal breathlessness warrant medical advice before training harder.
What these figures do not say
  • The FRIEND values, the age thresholds and the 12-minute Cooper table come from secondary sources; the origin of the Cooper Institute sample is not described.
  • The 52.2-metre threshold comes from 15 male amateur runners: it cannot be transposed as is to a woman, a beginner or another test.
  • The ACSM, EUROFIT, ALPHA-Fitness and FITNESSGRAM norm tables are not assessed here.

Frequently asked questions

Which norm table should I use?

The one for your sex, your age bracket and your type of test, whose sample and year you know. If several exist, note them all: if your conclusion changes, do not draw a strong conclusion from it.

Is a 50th percentile good?

It is the median of your reference group, nothing more. What it is worth for health depends on what that group is: a healthy population, patients, a laboratory sample.1,6

My score dropped by 1 point: should I worry?

Not on a single test. Compare the difference with the error of your own test: for the 12-minute Cooper, one study uses 52.2 metres in amateur runners; for you, the value is only known if you redo it.16
